name: Norman Foster
bio: From a working-class Manchester terrace to Yale, a partnership with Richard Rogers, and eventually the House of Lords, Foster industrialized elegance and built the largest architectural practice of his era on it. The early sheds for Reliance Controls and Willis Faber proved that lightweight structure and daylight could be a corporate ethic; the Hongkong Bank spent an unprecedented budget proving it at skyscraper scale. His office went on to reshape airports, parliaments, bridges and the London skyline, always with the same conviction that technology is a form of optimism. A pilot who still sketches from the cockpit, he treats flight — light structure defeating gravity — as the discipline's founding metaphor.

projects.title: HSBC Headquarters
projects.blurb: A suspended-structure bank, famously the most expensive building of its day.

projects.title: 30 St Mary Axe
projects.blurb: The Gherkin — a ventilating diagrid cone that changed London's skyline.

projects.title: Reichstag Dome
projects.blurb: A glass dome with a public spiral above the reunified parliament.

projects.title: Millau Viaduct
projects.blurb: The tallest bridge in the world, light as a line drawing.

projects.title: Hong Kong Airport
projects.blurb: A single lightweight roof over what was then the world's largest enclosed space.

projects.title: Sainsbury Centre
projects.blurb: An early hangar for art with services buried in its deep walls.

projects.title: Great Court, British Museum
projects.blurb: A torus glass roof turning a leftover courtyard into London's largest covered square.

projects.title: Apple Park
projects.blurb: A mile-round glass ring in a rebuilt Californian landscape.

projects.title: Commerzbank Tower
projects.blurb: The first ecological skyscraper — sky gardens spiraling up a triangular plan.

projects.title: Willis Faber & Dumas
projects.blurb: A black glass amoeba with a rooftop lawn and a swimming pool for staff.

name: Glenn Murcutt
bio: Born in London and raised partly in Papua New Guinea by a gold-prospecting father who read him Thoreau, Murcutt has practiced alone in Sydney since 1969 — no partners, no staff, no website, a waiting list measured in years. His subject is almost always the house, and his method is a marriage of the Farnsworth plan with the Australian woolshed: corrugated iron, louvres, verandahs, buildings tuned to breeze, water and bushfire long before sustainability was a word. The motto he borrowed from Aboriginal usage, touch this earth lightly, is engineering instruction rather than sentiment; many of his houses can be read as instruments for their climate. The 2002 Pritzker went, for once, to an architect with no airport, no museum and no publicity apparatus, and his annual master classes have exported the discipline of drawing by hand and thinking by section to several generations.

projects.title: Magney House
projects.blurb: A single corrugated-steel wave of roof on the coastal grassland, collecting its own water; the clearest statement of his rural house type.

projects.title: Marie Short House
projects.blurb: Two timber pavilions on a farm floodplain, the breakthrough that crossed Mies with the woolshed; Murcutt later bought it himself.

projects.title: Simpson-Lee House
projects.blurb: A near-ascetic glass and steel house in the Blue Mountains for clients who asked for less; its ponds double as bushfire reservoirs.

projects.title: Marika–Alderton House
projects.blurb: A house for a Yolngu artist in Arnhem Land with no glass at all — plywood flaps open the whole envelope to the tropical air.

projects.title: Australian Islamic Centre
projects.blurb: A mosque without minaret or dome, lit by 96 roof lanterns; designed with Hakan Elevli over a decade of community consultation.

projects.title: Boyd Education Centre
projects.blurb: An artists' residence and hall above the Shoalhaven River, designed with Wendy Lewin and Reg Lark; his largest public commission for years.

projects.title: Ball-Eastaway House
projects.blurb: A steel tube for two painters, floated over sandstone so the bush runs untouched beneath.

projects.title: Fredericks House
projects.blurb: A farmhouse of parallel sheds that refined the verandah-and-louvre vocabulary of the early houses.

projects.title: Berowra Waters Inn
projects.blurb: A restaurant reachable only by boat, remade as a quiet glass pavilion against a sandstone escarpment.

projects.title: MPavilion
projects.blurb: His first Melbourne building and rare temporary work — a thin white wing of a roof for a summer program of talks.

name: Peter Cook
bio: Cook founded the Archigram broadsheet in 1961 with five fellow London malcontents and spent the decade drawing the cities the profession was afraid of — plug-in megastructures, walking machines, instant festivals delivered by balloon. Almost none of it was built, which was partly the point; the drawings themselves rewired architecture's imagination and fed everything from the Pompidou to high-tech at large. He then taught for half a century — the AA, the Städelschule, chair of the Bartlett, which he rebuilt into a drawing-mad powerhouse — while Archigram collected the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 2002 as a group. His first major building, the blue biomorphic Kunsthaus Graz with Colin Fournier, arrived when he was 66, and with Gavin Robotham's CRAB Studio he has kept building in loud color ever since, knighted and entirely unrepentant.

projects.title: Plug-in City
projects.blurb: The Archigram project — a crane-tended megastructure of replaceable capsule dwellings that made obsolescence a design principle.

projects.title: Kunsthaus Graz
projects.blurb: The friendly alien — a blue acrylic blob with light-nozzle snouts, designed with Colin Fournier, landing among red-tiled roofs.

projects.title: Instant City
projects.blurb: Airships descend on a sleepy town, deliver a metropolis of media and events, then move on; pop culture as urban infrastructure.

projects.title: Abedian School of Architecture
projects.blurb: A CRAB Studio building for teaching architecture — concrete scoops and verandah-like decks arranged around a central street of crits.

projects.title: Drawing Studio
projects.blurb: A small crinkled blue steel vessel for the Arts University — a manifesto for drawing by the profession's great draughtsman.

projects.title: Law & Central Administration Building, Campus WU
projects.blurb: Orange-and-yellow wrapped faculties for the Vienna University of Economics, on a campus shared with Hadid and Holl.

projects.title: Montreal Entertainments Tower
projects.blurb: An early Archigram tower of stacked auditoria and fairground programs proposed for Expo 67.

projects.title: Blow-out Village
projects.blurb: A hovercraft-borne village that inflates on arrival — disaster relief and seaside leisure in one pneumatic package.

projects.title: IBA Housing, Lützowplatz
projects.blurb: Social housing with Christine Hawley for the Berlin building exhibition — a rare early chance to build the layered facades he drew.

projects.title: Arcadia
projects.blurb: A decade of drawings dissolving the megastructure into terraces and vegetation; the city softening into landscape.

name: Renzo Piano
bio: Son of a Genoese builder, Piano was 33 when he and Richard Rogers won the Pompidou competition and scandalized Paris with an inside-out culture machine; he has spent the fifty years since demonstrating that the same structural intelligence can whisper. The Building Workshop, run from a glass hillside studio outside Genoa and an office in Paris, is organized like a craft shop: every project begins with the piece, the joint, the way light comes down. Its range is almost unreasonable — a Pacific cultural center of timber cases, a floating airport terminal, the tallest tower in western Europe — held together by lightness and an allergy to rhetoric. Pritzker laureate in 1998 and an Italian senator for life since 2013, he channels his senator's salary into G124, a small team repairing the peripheries of Italian cities.

projects.title: Centre Pompidou
projects.blurb: With Richard Rogers — the building turned inside out, structure and services on the facade and a free public piazza in front.

projects.title: Menil Collection
projects.blurb: A quiet museum under a roof of ferrocement light-leaves; the counter-argument to Beaubourg from the same hand.

projects.title: Kansai Airport Terminal
projects.blurb: A mile-long wing of a terminal on an artificial island, its roof shaped by the air moving through it.

projects.title: Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre
projects.blurb: Ten timber cases derived from Kanak huts, open to the trade winds — high-tech in the service of another culture's memory.

projects.title: The Shard
projects.blurb: A tapering glass spire over London Bridge station, sketched first on a restaurant napkin and long western Europe's tallest building.

projects.title: Fondation Beyeler
projects.blurb: Long stone walls and a glass light-roof for a dealer's collection; museum-making reduced to wall, light and garden.

projects.title: Whitney Museum
projects.blurb: An industrial-scaled ship of galleries and terraces at the foot of the High Line.

projects.title: California Academy of Sciences
projects.blurb: A natural history museum under a living green roof that rolls like the park's own topography.

projects.title: Auditorium Parco della Musica
projects.blurb: Three lead-clad concert halls arranged like beetles around an open amphitheater.

projects.title: The New York Times Building
projects.blurb: A ceramic-rod veil over a Manhattan tower, designed to change color with the sky.

name: Rafael Moneo
bio: From Tudela in Navarre, Moneo apprenticed with Sáenz de Oíza in Madrid and then with Jørn Utzon in Denmark while the Sydney Opera House was on the boards, and came away convinced that buildings outlive their architects' intentions. He is the profession's great scholar-practitioner: decades of teaching in Madrid and Barcelona, chair of Harvard's GSD from 1985 to 1990, and essays on typology and his contemporaries that are read as closely as his plans. The Roman museum at Mérida — monumental brick arcades striding over the excavations they protect — made the argument that new architecture can think in an ancient language without costume. Spain's first Pritzker laureate, in 1996, he builds slowly and city by city: a station, a cathedral, a museum extension, each answering its site rather than his signature.

projects.title: National Museum of Roman Art
projects.blurb: Parallel walls of Roman-format brick arching over an active excavation; modern construction speaking fluent antiquity.

projects.title: Kursaal
projects.blurb: Two tilted translucent glass cubes — beached rocks, he called them — holding an auditorium and congress hall at the river mouth.

projects.title: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels
projects.blurb: An adobe-colored concrete cathedral of oblique geometries and alabaster light beside the Hollywood Freeway.
projects.wikipedia: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels

projects.title: Atocha Station Extension
projects.blurb: A new high-speed terminal that turned the nineteenth-century train shed into a palm-house garden.

projects.title: Prado Museum Extension
projects.blurb: An underground link and cloister addition that enlarged Spain's national gallery almost invisibly.

projects.title: Moderna Museet & Arkitekturmuseet
projects.blurb: Sweden's modern art and architecture museums as a low village of lantern-roofed rooms on Skeppsholmen island.

projects.title: Pilar and Joan Miró Foundation
projects.blurb: A fortified concrete star of galleries guarding Miró's studios against the encroaching resort coast.

projects.title: Bankinter Building
projects.blurb: With Ramón Bescós — a taut brick bank behind a preserved villa, the founding work of Madrid's contextual modernism.

projects.title: Murcia City Hall Annex
projects.blurb: A civic facade composed like a stone retable, holding its own on a baroque cathedral square.

projects.title: Audrey Jones Beck Building
projects.blurb: A limestone gallery block for the Museum of Fine Arts, lit by a roofscape of angled light scoops.

name: Moshe Safdie
bio: Born in Haifa and transplanted to Montreal at fifteen, Safdie turned his McGill student thesis into Habitat 67, the stacked-box housing hill of Expo 67, and was world-famous at 29 — a debut so complete he spent decades both chasing and escaping it. The slogan behind it, for everyone a garden, has remained the program: density that still delivers light, terraces and sky to ordinary dwellings. After 1967 he opened a Jerusalem branch and shaped swaths of the city, from the Mamilla quarter to the descending concrete prism of Yad Vashem's Holocaust History Museum. From his Boston practice came North American civic staples — Ottawa's National Gallery, Vancouver's library — and then the Asian megaprojects, Marina Bay Sands and Jewel Changi, which made him the rare octogenarian architect whose buildings double as national logos.

projects.title: Habitat 67
projects.blurb: 354 prefabricated concrete boxes stacked into a housing hillside for Expo 67 — a student thesis that became modern housing's most famous experiment.

projects.title: Marina Bay Sands
projects.blurb: Three 55-storey towers carrying a shared SkyPark and cantilevered pool; instantly the shorthand image of Singapore.

projects.title: Jewel Changi Airport
projects.blurb: A glass torus over an indoor forest and a seven-storey ring waterfall, grafted onto an airport interchange.

projects.title: Yad Vashem Holocaust History Museum
projects.blurb: A concrete prism cut through the Mount of Remembrance, erupting into daylight over the Jerusalem forest.

projects.title: National Gallery of Canada
projects.blurb: A granite and glass gallery whose crystalline Great Hall answers the Parliament library across the gorge.

projects.title: Crystal Bridges Museum
projects.blurb: Pavilions with suspended timber roofs bridging two spring-fed ponds in an Ozark ravine.
projects.wikipedia: Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art

projects.title: Kauffman Center for the Performing Arts
projects.blurb: Two shells of stacked steel arcs behind a cable-stayed glass foyer overlooking the city.
projects.wikipedia: Kauffman Center for the Performing Arts

projects.title: Vancouver Public Library
projects.blurb: A library wrapped in a spiraling colonnade wall the public promptly nicknamed the Colosseum.

projects.title: Virasat-e-Khalsa
projects.blurb: A museum of Sikh history — clustered sandstone petals with stainless roofs, bridging a ravine toward the fortress town.

projects.title: Raffles City Chongqing
projects.blurb: Eight towers at the Yangtze confluence, four of them carrying a 300-meter horizontal skybridge conservatory.

name: Ricardo Bofill
bio: A builder's son expelled from Barcelona's architecture school for leftist agitation under Franco, Bofill finished his training in Geneva and at 23 founded the Taller de Arquitectura — a deliberately mixed workshop of architects, poets, mathematicians and a film-maker. Its early Spanish work turned housing into casbah-like geometric games, most photogenically the red-walled Muralla Roja above the Calpe coast; its headquarters was a disused cement factory he spent fifty years converting into a cypress-wrapped palace-studio. In France he swerved into monumental prefabricated classicism, casting columns and pediments in concrete to give new-town social housing the scale of Versailles — postmodernism at its most operatic, later a dystopian film set of choice. The practice's later corporate decades were tamer, but the 1970s and 80s work has been rediscovered by a generation raised on its photographs. He died of Covid in Barcelona in January 2022, the Taller continuing under his sons.

projects.title: La Muralla Roja
projects.blurb: A red-and-pink casbah of interlocking stairs and terraces above the Mediterranean; the internet's favorite Bofill.

projects.title: Walden 7
projects.blurb: A rust-red vertical labyrinth of 446 apartments around interior courtyards, named after a utopian novel.

projects.title: Les Espaces d'Abraxas
projects.blurb: Social housing as prefab-concrete theater, palace and arch outside Paris; Brazil and The Hunger Games both shot here.

projects.title: La Fábrica
projects.blurb: A ruined cement factory remade over decades as the Taller's studio and Bofill's own home — silos as offices, kiln hall as cathedral.

projects.title: Antigone
projects.blurb: A kilometer-long neoclassical district on axis to the river — an entire quarter composed like a baroque plan.

projects.title: Les Arcades du Lac
projects.blurb: The first French monumental housing scheme, its lakeside wing a Versailles aqueduct with apartments inside.

projects.title: Kafka Castle
projects.blurb: An early cellular experiment — holiday apartments clustered like cubic crystals on a hill, named for the novel.

projects.title: National Theatre of Catalonia
projects.blurb: A glass Parthenon for the Catalan stage — classical temple envelope, modern machinery within.

projects.title: 77 West Wacker Drive
projects.blurb: His American corporate turn — a white postmodern-classical tower on the Chicago River.

projects.title: W Barcelona
projects.blurb: A glass sail of a hotel planted at the end of the Barceloneta breakwater, redrawing the city's sea front.

name: Tadao Ando
bio: A former boxer from Osaka with no formal training, Ando taught himself architecture from books and long pilgrimages to the buildings of Europe, then opened an office and began winning against the credentialed world almost immediately. The tiny Row House in Sumiyoshi announced the program: smooth-cast concrete, geometric severity, and a willingness to make inhabitants cross open air in the rain for the sake of living with the weather. Churches, museums and whole islands followed — above all Naoshima, where his buried galleries turned an industrial backwater into an art-world destination. Across fifty years the palette has barely changed; the conviction that emptiness, light and material silence are architecture's real subjects has only deepened.

projects.title: Church of the Light
projects.blurb: A concrete box split by a cruciform slot of daylight.

projects.title: Row House in Sumiyoshi
projects.blurb: The tiny courtyard house that made his name — you cross open air to reach the bedroom.

projects.title: Chichu Art Museum
projects.blurb: A museum buried in an island hilltop, lit only from above.

projects.title: Water Temple
projects.blurb: Entry by descending through a lotus pond.

projects.title: Koshino House
projects.blurb: Parallel concrete bars set into a slope, tuned to raking light.

projects.title: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth
projects.blurb: Glass pavilions standing in a reflecting pool beside Kahn's Kimbell.
projects.wikipedia: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth

projects.title: Punta della Dogana
projects.blurb: A customs house remade for the Pinault collection — new concrete inside old brick.

projects.title: Church on the Water
projects.blurb: A chapel whose fourth wall slides away toward a cross in a pond.

projects.title: Galleria Akka
projects.blurb: Urban infill as carved concrete canyon.

projects.title: Bourse de Commerce
projects.blurb: A concrete cylinder inserted beneath a nineteenth-century dome.

name: Toyo Ito
bio: Born in Japanese-occupied Seoul in 1941 and trained under the Metabolist Kiyonori Kikutake, Ito opened his own Tokyo office in 1971 under the name Urban Robot and spent the 1980s theorizing an architecture as light and provisional as the media city around it. The White U, a windowless ring house for his widowed sister, and his own Silver Hut set the private groundwork; the Tower of Winds turned a ventilation shaft into an urban instrument flickering with the city's noise. Sendai Mediatheque, its floors threaded on swaying tubes of white steel like seaweed, redefined the public building for the digital age — and rode out the 2011 earthquake on camera. After the tsunami he built Home-for-All communal shelters in the disaster zone, a self-critical turn he called architecture's social re-founding. The 2013 Pritzker acknowledged both the buildings and a mentor's shadow: Sejima, Nishizawa and much of Japan's present generation passed through his orbit.

projects.title: Sendai Mediatheque
projects.blurb: Seven floor plates threaded on thirteen swaying lattice tubes — library and gallery reimagined as transparent public infrastructure.

projects.title: Tower of Winds
projects.blurb: A ventilation tower wrapped in perforated aluminum, its lights driven by wind and city noise; media architecture before the term.

projects.title: White U
projects.blurb: A windowless ring of a house built for his grieving sister, inward-looking to the point of monasticism; later demolished, as he intended.

projects.title: Silver Hut
projects.blurb: His own house of vaulted aluminum lightness, since re-erected as part of his museum in Imabari.

projects.title: Tod's Omotesando Building
projects.blurb: A boutique whose concrete structure traces overlapping zelkova-tree silhouettes — facade, structure and sign in one.

projects.title: Tama Art University Library
projects.blurb: Colonnades of impossibly thin concrete arches sliding past each other on a sloping ground floor.

projects.title: National Taichung Theater
projects.blurb: An opera house of continuous curved concrete membranes — caves for sound with almost no straight walls.

projects.title: Serpentine Gallery Pavilion
projects.blurb: With Cecil Balmond — a box whose apparently random faceted structure derives from an algorithm of rotating squares.

projects.title: Gifu Media Cosmos
projects.blurb: A library under an undulating latticed timber roof, its reading rooms gathered beneath fabric funnels of light.

projects.title: Toyo Ito Museum of Architecture
projects.blurb: Steel polyhedra on an island slope holding his archive — Japan's first museum dedicated to a single architect.

name: Peter Zumthor
bio: Trained first as a cabinetmaker and then as a conservator of historic villages, Zumthor settled in Haldenstein in the Graubünden and built a practice on the refusal to hurry. His office stays small, takes few commissions, keeps no website, and works on buildings for a decade or more; what emerges is measured in temperature, sound and smell as much as in meters. The baths at Vals made bathing liturgical; Bregenz made an art museum out of veiled light; the Bruder Klaus chapel was cast around a burning wigwam of tree trunks by the farmers who would pray in it. The Pritzker jury called his work permanent; his admirers treat visiting it as pilgrimage, which is roughly what he intends.

projects.title: Therme Vals
projects.blurb: A bath of layered quartzite half-buried in an alpine slope.

projects.title: Kunsthaus Bregenz
projects.blurb: A frosted-glass lantern for art on the shore of Lake Constance.

projects.title: Bruder Klaus Field Chapel

projects.title: Kolumba Museum
projects.blurb: Grey brick knitting a ruined Gothic church into a museum of quiet rooms.

projects.title: Saint Benedict Chapel

projects.title: Zinc Mine Museum

projects.title: Steilneset Memorial
